# Campfire

Campfire is a web-based chat application. It supports many of the features you'd
expect, including:

- Multiple rooms, with access controls
- Direct messages
- File attachments with previews
- Search
- Notifications (via Web Push)
- @mentions

## Running your own Campfire instance

Campfire's Docker image contains everything needed for a fully-functional,
single-machine deployment. This includes the web app, background jobs, caching,
file serving, and SSL. You can use our pre-built image at
`ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire:latest`, or build your own from this repo.

### Deploying with ONCE

The easiest way to self-host Campfire is with [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once).
It will guide you through the initial set up and then keep your instance up to date automatically.

If you don't already have `once` installed, run this on the machine you want to run Campfire on:

```sh
curl https://get.once.com | sh
```

`once` will launch as soon as the install is finished. 

Choose Campfire from the list of applications, follow the instructions, and ONCE will take care of the rest.

If you prefer the command line to the dashboard, you can deploy directly:

```sh
once deploy ghcr.io/basecamp/once-campfire --host chat.example.com
```

### Deploying with Docker

If you'd rather run the Docker image yourself, you can read more about that in the [self-hosting guide](docs/self-hosting.md).

> [!TIP]
> When you start Campfire for the first time, you'll be guided through a wizard to create an admin account.
> The email address that you enter for the admin account will be visible on the sign-in page, it's there so
> that people have someone to contact if they need help with their account. If that bothers you, put in any
> email address you want and create yourself a new admin account.

## Development

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
Please see our [development guide](docs/development.md) for how to get Campfire set up for local development.

## Security

See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for how to report a vulnerability and a description of our trust model.

{ "returncode": 0, "output": "# Chat bots Bots are chat members that post messages over HTTP. They're aimed at shell scripts and CI jobs: a deploy script can announce that it finished, a test run can post its summary. ## Model - `Bot` (`bots` table) holds the bot's **code**, the credential that authenticates its requests, and its **creator** (the person who set it up). - Each bot has its own `User` (`bots.user_id`, one-to-one). That user carries the bot's name and avatar and is what messages, memberships and notifications point at. So a bot is an ordinary member as far as the rest of the app is concerned: it's named and avatared like anyone, shows as the author of its messages, joins open rooms when it's created, can be granted closed rooms like anyone, and triggers push notifications the same way. - The bot's user has no email address and a random password nobody knows. Bots never sign in, but the users table requires a password digest. - Deleting a bot (`User#deactivate`, which the bot's delete button and the account members list both use) deactivates its user, the same as for people, and destroys the `Bot` row. That removes the code, so the bot can't post, but its past messages stay attributed to it. - Bots are listed as members in the account's people list, the room member pickers and direct-message pickers, as people are. Removing a bot from the people list deactivates it, the same as deleting it on `/bots`. Changing a bot's role there has no effect, since bots never sign in. Permissions reuse `User#can_administer?(record)`, which already lets a record's creator or an administrator manage it. Any member can create bots. The list shows your own bots, or every bot for administrators. ## Web UI - `/account/edit` has a bot icon link ("Set up chat bots") for every member, not only administrators. - `/bots` lists the bots (no pagination). Each item shows the name, the creator (for administrators), an edit link ("Edit "), and a read-only "Bot code" field with a copy button. The page is marked `turbo-cache-control: no-cache` so Turbo doesn't keep codes in its page cache. - `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit` share one form: avatar (optional), name ("Name the bot", required), "Save changes". The edit page adds "Delete this chat bot", which asks for confirmation with Turbo's `data-turbo-confirm` (the native `confirm()`). - Forms that fail validation re-render with status 422. - An empty file field doesn't clear the current avatar. The controller drops blank `avatar` params. ## HTTP API ``` curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" \ https://chat.example.com/rooms///messages ``` Route: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages` (`bot_messages_path`), handled by `Bots::MessagesController`. | Situation | Status | |---------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------| | Message created | `201 Created`, `Location: /messages/:id` | | Unknown, deleted or banned bot code | `401 Unauthorized` | | Room doesn't exist, or the bot isn't a member of it | `404 Not Found` | | Empty or whitespace-only body and no attachment | `422 Unprocessable Content` | Checks run in that order, so an unknown code gets 401 whatever the room is. A response never includes the code. Request bodies: - **Any content type is taken as plain text.** The raw body is the message, with no JSON envelope and no field names. A body such as `100% done`, `a=b&c=d` or `{not json` is posted as written. Rails doesn't parse it (see below). - The text is trimmed, and line breaks (`\r\n` or `\n`) are kept as line breaks. - Invalid UTF-8 bytes are replaced with U+FFFD. - **Multipart** (`curl -F`) is the one exception: its `attachment` file becomes the message, the way a person's file upload does. A message is either text or a file, as in the web app, so any text in a multipart request is ignored and a multipart request without an attachment is a 422. Message content: the text is HTML-escaped before it's stored as rich text, so markup in it is shown literally, and URLs still autolink like anywhere else. Newlines are stored as `
` so they show up in the message. Once created, the message goes through the same path as a person's: it's broadcast to the room (`Message#broadcast_create`), marks the room unread for members, and enqueues `Room::PushMessageJob`. ## Security notes - **The code is a credential.** It's 24 random base58 characters (`has_secure_token`), unique, and stored as-is, because the list has to show it. Anyone who holds it can post as the bot, so: - It's only shown to the bot's creator and to administrators, on `/bots`. Edit and delete pages don't show it. - It travels in the URL path, which is why it's masked everywhere a path or URL gets recorded: - Request logs: `lib/rails_ext/request_filtered_path.rb` prepends to `ActionDispatch::Request#filtered_path`, and `BotCodeFilter` masks `/rooms/:id//messages`. Parameter logs mask `code` (`filter_parameter_logging.rb`). - Sentry: `config/initializers/sentry.rb` scrubs the request URL in `before_send`. - Deactivating a user, or banning one, stops its bots from authenticating (`Bot.authenticate` only accepts active users). - The endpoint is outside the session and CSRF machinery: `allow_unauthenticated_access`, `skip_forgery_protection`. - Rails' parameter parsing is skipped for the body (`Bots::MessagesController#process_action`). Otherwise Rails parses form bodies (`100% done` is an invalid form, so it gets a 400) and JSON bodies (malformed JSON gets a 400). Multipart requests are still parsed, for the attachment. - Bot text is HTML-escaped before it's stored, so bots can't inject markup into other people's pages. ## Known limits and follow-ups - The code isn't encrypted at rest. The app doesn't configure Active Record encryption keys, and the code has to be shown on the list. Adding encryption would mean adding keys to deployments, and `find_by(code:)` would need deterministic encryption. - There's no way to rotate a code yet. Deleting and recreating the bot is the workaround. A "Regenerate code" action is the natural next step. - No rate limiting on the bot endpoint. A leaked code can flood a room until its bot is deleted. - SQL debug logs show the literal values SQLite queries use, including bot codes and session tokens, so don't run production at `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug`. - Bot-authored messages don't show a "bot" badge. The author name is the only marker. - Neither bot text nor attachments have a size limit, the same as people's messages. A very large body is read into memory in full. - System tests need a chromedriver. They didn't run in the sandbox this was built in (it has no network to download one), so the UI was checked with controller tests and by driving the running app over HTTP. ---- ## Development ### Setting up First, get everything installed and configured with: ```sh bin/setup ``` This installs the system packages Campfire needs (SQLite, ffmpeg), the right Ruby version (via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev)), and the app's gems; prepares the database; and starts Redis (in a Docker container called `campfire-redis`, if it isn't already running locally). If you want to start over at any point, run: ```sh bin/setup --reset ``` ### Running the server Start the development server with: ```sh bin/dev ``` You'll be able to access the app at http://localhost:3000. On first run you'll be guided through creating your admin account, and you can sign in with that account from then on. Note that Campfire needs Redis (for Action Cable, caching, and background jobs), so if you've restarted your machine or stopped the container, `docker start campfire-redis` will bring it back. ### Web Push notifications Campfire uses VAPID (Voluntary Application Server Identification) keys to send browser push notifications. For notifications to work in development you'll need to generate a key pair and set these environment variables: - `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY` - `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY` You can generate a fresh pair (along with a secret key base, which you can ignore in development) by running: ```sh script/admin/generate-secrets ``` ### Running tests Run the unit tests with: ```sh bin/rails test ``` And the browser-based system tests with: ```sh bin/rails test:system ``` Before pushing your changes, you can run the full CI suite locally - style checks, security audits, and all the tests - with a single command: ```sh bin/ci ``` ### Contributing You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking. If you'd like to contribute your changes back, please read our [contributing guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first. " }

Bot.all : Current.user.bots end # A file field submits nothing when no file is chosen, which must not clear the current avatar. def bot_params params.require(:bot).permit(:name, :avatar).reject { |key, value| key == "avatar" && value.blank? } end end === app/controllers/bots/messages_controller.rb # Lets bots post messages from scripts and CI jobs. The bot code in the path is the only credential, and the # raw request body is the message: no JSON envelope, no field names. Multipart uploads are the one exception: their # `attachment` file becomes the message, as it does when a person posts a file. class Bots::MessagesController < ApplicationController include ActiveStorage::SetCurrent allow_unauthenticated_access skip_forgery_protection before_action :set_bot, :set_room, :ensure_content_present def create message = @room.messages.create_with_attachment!(message_attributes) message.broadcast_create head :created, location: message_path(message) end private # The body is the message, not parameters. Left alone, Rails would parse it as a form or JSON document # before any action runs, and a body such as "100% done" would be rejected with a 400. Multipart is the # exception, since its attachment has to be parsed. def process_action(*) request.request_parameters = {} unless multipart? super end def set_bot @bot = Bot.authenticate(params[:bot_code]) head :unauthorized unless @bot end def set_room @room = @bot.user.rooms.find_by(id: params[:room_id]) head :not_found unless @room end def ensure_content_present head :unprocessable_content if message_text.blank? && uploaded_attachment.nil? end def message_attributes { creator: @bot.user, body: (message_html if message_text.present?), attachment: uploaded_attachment }.compact end # Bot text is plain text, so it's escaped before being stored as rich text: markup in it is shown as written. def message_html ERB::Util.html_escape(message_text).gsub("\n", "
") end # Like the web app, a message is either text or a file, so a multipart request carries no text. def message_text @message_text ||= (multipart? ? "" : request_text).gsub(/\r\n?/, "\n").strip end def request_text request.raw_post.dup.force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8).scrub end def uploaded_attachment params[:attachment] if multipart? && params[:attachment].is_a?(ActionDispatch::Http::UploadedFile) end def multipart? request.media_type == "multipart/form-data" end end === app/helpers/bots_helper.rb module BotsHelper def bot_avatar_tag(bot, **options) if bot.user&.persisted? image_tag fresh_user_avatar_path(bot.user), **options else image_tag "default-avatar.svg", **options end end end === lib/bot_code_filter.rb # Bot codes are credentials carried in the path of every bot message (POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages), # so anything that records request paths or URLs has to mask them. module BotCodeFilter MASK = "[FILTERED]" PATTERN = %r{(/rooms/[^/?#]+/)[^/?#]+(/messages\b)} def self.filter(path_or_url) path_or_url.to_s.gsub(PATTERN, "\\1#{MASK}\\2") end end === lib/rails_ext/request_filtered_path.rb # Rails logs request.filtered_path, which only masks query parameters. Bot codes sit in the path, so mask them here too. module BotCodeFilteredPath def filtered_path BotCodeFilter.filter(super) end end ActionDispatch::Request.prepend BotCodeFilteredPath app/controllers/bots: messages_controller.rb app/views/bots: _bot.html.erb _form.html.erb edit.html.erb index.html.erb new.html.erb " }

class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do
    def grant_to(users)
      room = proxy_association.owner
      Membership.insert_all(Array(users).collect { |user| { room_id: room.id, user_id: user.id, involvement: room.default_involvement } })
    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

    def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
      transaction do
        grant_to(granted) if granted.present?
        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end
  end

  has_many :users, through: :memberships
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validate :direct_rooms_keep_their_type, on: :update

  scope :opens,           -> { where(type: "Rooms::Open") }
  scope :closeds,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Closed") }
  scope :directs,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Direct") }
  scope :without_directs, -> { where.not(type: "Rooms::Direct") }

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }

  class << self
    def create_for(attributes, users:)
      transaction do
        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

    def original
      order(:created_at).first
    end
  end

  def receive(message)
    unread_memberships(message)
    push_later(message)
  end

  def open?
    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

  def closed?
    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

  def direct?
    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

  def default_involvement
    "mentions"
  end

  private
    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other freely. A direct room can't become
    # either: its participants agreed to a private conversation, not to one whose
    # audience someone else gets to widen afterwards.
    def direct_rooms_keep_their_type
      if type_changed? && type_was == "Rooms::Direct"
        errors.add :type, "can't be changed for a direct room"
      end
    end

    def unread_memberships(message)
      memberships.visible.disconnected.where.not(user: message.creator).update_all(unread_at: message.created_at, updated_at: Time.current)
    end

    def push_later(message)
      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)
    end
end

class Room::MessagePusher
  attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload
      end
    end

    def build_direct_payload
      {
        title: message.creator.name,
        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(message.mentionees)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_everything)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(mentionees)
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_mentions).where(user_id: mentionees.ids)
    end

    def relevant_subscriptions
      Push::Subscription
        .joins(user: :memberships)
        .merge(Membership.visible.disconnected.where(room: room).where.not(user: message.creator))
    end

    def enqueue_payload_for_delivery(payload, subscriptions)
      Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.queue(payload, subscriptions)
    end
end

# This is in lib so we can use it in a thread pool without the Rails executor
class WebPush::Pool
  attr_reader :delivery_pool, :invalidation_pool, :connection, :invalid_subscription_handler

  def initialize(invalid_subscription_handler:)
    @delivery_pool = Concurrent::ThreadPoolExecutor.new(max_threads: 50, queue_size: 10000)
    @invalidation_pool = Concurrent::FixedThreadPool.new(1)
    @connection = Net::HTTP::Persistent.new(name: "web_push", pool_size: 150)
    @invalid_subscription_handler = invalid_subscription_handler
  end

  def queue(payload, subscriptions)
    subscriptions.find_each do |subscription|
      deliver_later(payload, subscription)
    end
  end

  def shutdown
    connection.shutdown
    shutdown_pool(delivery_pool)
    shutdown_pool(invalidation_pool)
  end

  private
    def deliver_later(payload, subscription)
      # Ensure any AR operations happen before we post to the thread pool
      notification = subscription.notification(**payload)
      subscription_id = subscription.id

      delivery_pool.post do
        deliver(notification, subscription_id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.deliver: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    rescue Concurrent::RejectedExecutionError
    end

    def deliver(notification, id)
      notification.deliver(connection: connection)
    rescue WebPush::ExpiredSubscription, OpenSSL::OpenSSLError => ex
      invalidate_subscription_later(id) if invalid_subscription_handler
    end

    def invalidate_subscription_later(id)
      invalidation_pool.post do
        invalid_subscription_handler.call(id)
      rescue Exception => e
        Rails.logger.error "Error in WebPush::Pool.invalid_subscription_handler: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
      end
    end

    def shutdown_pool(pool)
      pool.shutdown
      pool.kill unless pool.wait_for_termination(1)
    end
end

  def deliver(connection: nil)

      message: encoded_message,

    end

require "surfguard"

module RestrictedHTTP
  class Violation < StandardError; end

  # The address policy lives in the surfguard gem so this app, Basecamp, HEY and
  # Fizzy classify "internal" the same way instead of each keeping a copy that
  # drifts. The callers here hand a bare hostname in and pin the address that
  # comes back, so this stays a hostname-in, address-out shim.
  module PrivateNetworkGuard
    extend self

    # A hostname that resolves to nothing (NXDOMAIN, timeout, empty answer)
    # raises Surfguard::Unresolvable, which we let propagate as a lookup failure
    # -- the same way the old Resolv.getaddress guard raised Resolv::ResolvError,
    # and the callers here already treat it as a fetch failure. The Violation is
    # reserved for a host that resolves to a blocked address (an empty list back
    # from resolve_public_ips), so a transient DNS miss is never misreported as
    # an SSRF attempt.
    def resolve(hostname)
      Surfguard.resolve_public_ips(hostname).first or
        raise Violation.new("Attempt to access private IP via #{hostname}")
    end

    def private_ip?(ip)
      Surfguard.blocked_address?(ip)
    end
  end
end

require "restricted_http/private_network_guard"

class Opengraph::Fetch
  ALLOWED_DOCUMENT_CONTENT_TYPE = "text/html"
  MAX_BODY_SIZE = 5.megabytes
  MAX_REDIRECTS = 10

  class TooManyRedirectsError < StandardError; end
  class RedirectDeniedError < StandardError; end

  def fetch_document(url, ip: RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(url.host))
    request(url, Net::HTTP::Get, ip: ip) do |response|
      return body_if_acceptable(response)
    end
  end

  def fetch_content_type(url, ip: RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(url.host))
    request(url, Net::HTTP::Head, ip: ip) do |response|
      return response["Content-Type"]
    end
  end

  private
    def request(url, request_class, ip:)
      MAX_REDIRECTS.times do
        Net::HTTP.start(url.host, url.port, ipaddr: ip, use_ssl: url.scheme == "https") do |http|
          http.request request_class.new(url) do |response|
            if response.is_a?(Net::HTTPRedirection)
              url, ip = resolve_redirect(response["location"])
            else
              yield response
            end
          end
        end
      end

      raise TooManyRedirectsError
    end

    def resolve_redirect(location)
      url = URI.parse(location)
      raise RedirectDeniedError unless url.is_a?(URI::HTTP)
      [ url, RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(url.host) ]
    end

    def body_if_acceptable(response)
      size_restricted_body(response) if response_valid?(response)
    end

    def size_restricted_body(response)
      # We've already checked the Content-Length header, to try to avoid reading
      # the body of any large responses. But that header could be wrong or
      # missing. To be on the safe side, we'll read the body in chunks, and bail
      # if it runs over our size limit.
      StringIO.new.tap do |body|
        response.read_body do |chunk|
          return nil if body.string.bytesize + chunk.bytesize > MAX_BODY_SIZE
          body << chunk
        end
      end.string
    end

    def response_valid?(response)
      status_valid?(response) && content_type_valid?(response) && content_length_valid?(response)
    end

    def status_valid?(response)
      response.is_a?(Net::HTTPOK)
    end

    def content_type_valid?(response)
      response.content_type == ALLOWED_DOCUMENT_CONTENT_TYPE
    end

    def content_length_valid?(response)
      response.content_length.to_i <= MAX_BODY_SIZE
    end
end

class Opengraph::Location
  include ActiveModel::Validations

    fetch_html if valid? && !url.match(FILES_AND_MEDIA_URL_REGEX)

    Opengraph::Fetch.new.fetch_content_type(parsed_url, ip: resolved_ip) if valid?

    Rails.logger.warn "Failed to fetch #{parsed_url} at #{resolved_ip} (#{e})"
    nil
  end

    return @resolved_ip if defined? @resolved_ip
    @resolved_ip = RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(parsed_url.host) rescue nil

# Security

Report vulnerabilities through our [HackerOne program](https://hackerone.com/basecamp) or at
https://github.com/basecamp/once-campfire/security. Note that Campfire is in scope for our security
program, but is not bounty eligible.

## Trust model

Campfire is self-hosted and single-tenant, so the administrator is the server operator,
with shell, network, and database access already. Anything requiring the administrator
role grants nothing they do not already have, and is not a vulnerability.

We do want reports of anything a **non-administrator** can reach, and of any credential or
network path held by the Campfire process but not by the operator's own shell.

## Intentional behavior

Link unfurling can be triggered by any member pasting a URL, so it validates
destinations through `RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard`.

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "class ContentFilters::SanitizeAttributes < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    true
  end

  # Scrub attributes on the tags that SanitizeTags allows, using Rails' safe-list
  # sanitizer so unsafe URI schemes and event-handler attributes are stripped.
  # Runs after SanitizeTags, so passing the same allowed tags makes the tag pass
  # a no-op and only attributes are scrubbed.
  def apply
    sanitizer.sanitize fragment.to_html, tags: allowed_tags, attributes: allowed_attributes
  end

  private
    # Presentation styling relies on class attributes (e.g. unfurled link embeds),
    # which the standard ActionText set doesn't include.
    EXTRA_ALLOWED_ATTRIBUTES = %w[ class ]

    # ActionText::ContentHelper.sanitizer is a single process-wide instance, and
    # rails-html-sanitizer reuses one mutable permit scrubber that it reconfigures
    # from the tags/attributes on every #sanitize call. Sharing it here would race
    # our stricter tag set against ActionText's default rendering on concurrent
    # requests, so use a dedicated instance of the same sanitizer class to keep the
    # scrubber isolated.
    def sanitizer
      sanitizer_class.new
    end

    def sanitizer_class
      ActionText::ContentHelper.sanitizer.class
    end

    def allowed_tags
      ContentFilters::SanitizeTags::ALLOWED_TAGS
    end

    def allowed_attributes
      standard_allowed_attributes + EXTRA_ALLOWED_ATTRIBUTES
    end

    # Mirrors ActionText::ContentHelper#sanitizer_allowed_attributes, which isn't
    # exposed at the module level.
    def standard_allowed_attributes
      ActionText::ContentHelper.allowed_attributes ||
        (sanitizer_class.allowed_attributes + ActionText::Attachment::ATTRIBUTES).to_a
    end
end

module MessagesHelper
  def message_area_tag(room, &)
    tag.div id: "message-area", class: "message-area", contents: true, data: {
      controller: "messages presence drop-target",
      action: [ messages_actions, drop_target_actions, presence_actions ].join(" "),
      messages_first_of_day_class: "message--first-of-day",
      messages_formatted_class: "message--formatted",
      messages_me_class: "message--me",
      messages_mentioned_class: "message--mentioned",
      messages_threaded_class: "message--threaded",
      messages_page_url_value: room_messages_url(room)
    }, &
  end

  def messages_tag(room, &)
    tag.div id: dom_id(room, :messages), class: "messages", data: {
      controller: "maintain-scroll refresh-room",
      action: [ maintain_scroll_actions, refresh_room_actions ].join(" "),
      messages_target: "messages",
      refresh_room_loaded_at_value: room.updated_at.to_fs(:epoch),
      refresh_room_url_value: room_refresh_url(room)
    }, &
  end

  def message_tag(message, &)
    message_timestamp_milliseconds = message.created_at.to_fs(:epoch)

    tag.div id: dom_id(message),
      class: "message #{"message--emoji" if message.plain_text_body.all_emoji?}",
      data: {
        controller: "reply",
        user_id: message.creator_id,
        message_id: message.id,
        message_timestamp: message_timestamp_milliseconds,
        message_updated_at: message.updated_at.to_fs(:epoch),
        sort_value: message_timestamp_milliseconds,
        messages_target: "message",
        search_results_target: "message",
        refresh_room_target: "message",
        reply_composer_outlet: "#composer"
      }, &
  rescue Exception => e
    Sentry.capture_exception(e, extra: { message: message })
    Rails.logger.error "Exception while rendering message #{message.class.name}##{message.id}, failed with: #{e.class} `#{e.message}`"

    render "messages/unrenderable"
  end

  def message_timestamp(message, **attributes)
    local_datetime_tag message.created_at, **attributes
  end

  def message_presentation(message)
    case message.content_type
    when "attachment"
      message_attachment_presentation(message)
    when "sound"
      message_sound_presentation(message)
    else
      auto_link h(ContentFilters::TextMessagePresentationFilters.apply(message.body.body)), html: { target: "_blank" }
    end
  rescue Exception => e
    Sentry.capture_exception(e, extra: { message: message })
    Rails.logger.error "Exception while generating message representation for #{message.class.name}##{message.id}, failed with: #{e.class} `#{e.message}`"

    ""
  end

  private
    def messages_actions
      "turbo:before-stream-render@document->messages#beforeStreamRender keydown.up@document->messages#editMyLastMessage"
    end

    def maintain_scroll_actions
      "turbo:before-stream-render@document->maintain-scroll#beforeStreamRender"
    end

    def refresh_room_actions
      "visibilitychange@document->refresh-room#visibilityChanged online@window->refresh-room#online"
    end

    def presence_actions
      "visibilitychange@document->presence#visibilityChanged"
    end

    def message_attachment_presentation(message)
      Messages::AttachmentPresentation.new(message, context: self).render
    end

    def message_sound_presentation(message)
      sound = message.sound

      tag.div class: "sound", data: { controller: "sound", action: "messages:play->sound#play", sound_url_value: asset_path(sound.asset_path) } do
        play_button + (sound.image ? sound_image_tag(sound.image) : sound.text)
      end
    end

    def play_button
      tag.button "🔊", class: "btn btn--plain", data: { action: "sound#play" }
    end

    def sound_image_tag(image)
      image_tag image.asset_path, width: image.width, height: image.height, class: "align--middle"
    end

    def message_author_title(author)
      [ author.name, author.bio ].compact_blank.join(" – ")
    end
end

      filter.applicable? ? ActionText::Content.new(filter.apply, canonicalize: false) : content
    end

  def initialize(*filters)
    @filters = filters
  end

  def apply(content)
    filters.reduce(content) { |content, filter| filter.apply(content) }
  end

  private
    attr_reader :filters

steps.message: Next, the delivery class and the payload builder. The payload follows the format from the story, and the HTTP handling covers timeouts, the address guard, no redirects, capped reads, and the 200/204 rules.

require "net/http"
require "restricted_http/private_network_guard"

# Calls a bot's webhook when a message mentions the bot, and posts what the bot answers with:
#
# - 200 with text/plain or text/html: the body is posted into the room as the bot's message.
# - 204, or any other status: nothing is posted. A bot that wants to reply later can post over the bot API, using the
#   reply_to path in the payload.
#
# Bot::WebhookJob runs this, so a slow or broken webhook never holds up the person who posted the message.
class Bot::Webhook
  OPEN_TIMEOUT = 5.seconds
  READ_TIMEOUT = 10.seconds
  MAX_REPLY_SIZE = 1.megabyte
  REPLY_CONTENT_TYPES = %w[ text/plain text/html ]

  # Raised while reading a reply that's too big, to abandon the rest of the response.
  class ReplyTooLarge < StandardError; end

  # Failures reaching a bot are expected, so they're logged rather than retried. Anything else is a bug and raises.
  UNREACHABLE_ERRORS = [
    Timeout::Error, SocketError, SystemCallError, IOError, OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError,
    Net::ProtocolError, Net::HTTPBadResponse, Zlib::Error,
    RestrictedHTTP::Violation, Surfguard::Unresolvable
  ]

  attr_reader :bot, :message

  def initialize(bot, message)
    @bot, @message = bot, message
  end

  def deliver
    reply = fetch_reply

    post_reply(reply) if reply.present? && bot_in_room?
  rescue ReplyTooLarge, *UNREACHABLE_ERRORS => e
    Rails.logger.warn "Webhook for bot #{bot.id} produced no reply: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
  end

  private
    def url
      @url ||= URI.parse(bot.webhook_url)
    end

    # The address is checked and then pinned, so the connection goes to the address that was checked, even if DNS
    # changes in between. Redirects aren't followed, so a bot can't send us somewhere that wasn't checked.
    def fetch_reply
      ip = RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(url.host)

      Net::HTTP.start(url.host, url.port, ipaddr: ip, use_ssl: url.scheme == "https",
          open_timeout: OPEN_TIMEOUT.to_i, read_timeout: READ_TIMEOUT.to_i, write_timeout: READ_TIMEOUT.to_i) do |http|
        http.request(build_request) do |response|
          # Returning from inside the block means the body of anything but a 200 is never read.
          return response.is_a?(Net::HTTPOK) ? reply_html(response) : nil
        end
      end
    end

    def build_request
      Net::HTTP::Post.new(url, "Content-Type" => "application/json").tap do |request|
        request.body = Bot::Webhook::Payload.new(bot, message).to_json
      end
    end

    def reply_html(response)
      return unless REPLY_CONTENT_TYPES.include?(response.content_type&.downcase)

      text = decode(read_reply(response), response.type_params["charset"])

      if response.content_type.downcase == "text/html"
        Bot.html_from_html(text)
      else
        Bot.html_from_text(text)
      end
    end

    def read_reply(response)
      body = +""

      response.read_body do |chunk|
        body << chunk
        raise ReplyTooLarge if body.bytesize > MAX_REPLY_SIZE
      end

      body
    end

    # Falls back to UTF-8 when the reply names no charset, or one Ruby doesn't know.
    def decode(body, charset)
      encoding = Encoding.find(charset || "UTF-8") rescue Encoding::UTF_8

      body.force_encoding(encoding).encode(Encoding::UTF_8, invalid: :replace, undef: :replace)
    end

    # A bot that was removed from the room since the mention can't post into it, the same as over the bot API.
    def bot_in_room?
      bot.user.rooms.exists?(message.room_id)
    end

    def post_reply(html)
      # Only bot messages with visible text are posted. A reply of nothing but markup is left out.
      return unless ActionText::Content.new(html).to_plain_text.present?

      message.room.messages.create!(creator: bot.user, body: html).tap(&:broadcast_create)
    end
end
EOF
cat > app/models/bot/webhook/payload.rb <<'EOF'
# The JSON a bot's webhook receives when a message mentions it. Paths are relative: the bot knows its own Campfire
# origin. The reply_to path is the bot's own posting URL for the room, so a bot can reply later over the bot API.
class Bot::Webhook::Payload
  attr_reader :bot, :message

  delegate :room, to: :message

  def initialize(bot, message)
    @bot, @message = bot, message
  end

  def as_json(*)
    {
      event: "mention",
      author: { id: message.creator.id, name: message.creator.name },
      room: { id: room.id, name: room_name, reply_to: routes.bot_messages_path(room_id: room.id, bot_code: bot.code) },
      message: {
        id: message.id,
        body: { text: text, html: html },
        link: routes.room_at_message_path(room_id: room.id, message_id: message.id)
      }
    }
  end

  private
    def routes
      Rails.application.routes.url_helpers
    end

    # Direct rooms have no name of their own, so they're named after the people in them, other than the bot.
    def room_name
      if room.direct?
        room.users.without(bot.user).pluck(:name).to_sentence.presence
      else
        room.name
      end
    end

    # The text the bot is being asked, without the bot's own mention: "@Deploy Bot restart it" reads "restart it".
    # Mentions of other people stay as "@Name".
    def text
      content = message.body.body.fragment.replace(ActionText::Attachment.tag_name) do |node|
        ActionText::Attachable.from_node(node) == bot.user ? nil : node
      end

      ActionText::Content.new(content, canonicalize: false).to_plain_text.strip
    end

    def html
      message.body.to_s
    end
end
EOF

module Message::Mentionee
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  def mentionees
    room.users.where(id: mentioned_users.map(&:id))
  end

  # Bots mentioned in this message that are in its room, are active, and have a webhook. A bot's own messages mention
  # nothing for this purpose, since a bot's reply can mention another bot, and that would set off a loop.
  def mentioned_bots_with_webhooks
    return Bot.none if creator.bot

    Bot.joins(:user).merge(User.active).where(user: mentionees).where.not(webhook_url: nil)
  end

  # A check made when the message is created, so it doesn't look anything up: it only says whether the body has any
  # attachment that could be a mention.
  def may_mention_anyone?
    body.body&.fragment&.find_all(ActionText::Attachment.tag_name).present?
  end

  private
    def mentioned_users
      if body.body
        body.body.attachables.grep(User).uniq
      else
        []
      end
    end
end
EOF

# Calls the webhooks of the bots a message mentions. See Bot::Webhook.
class Bot::WebhookJob < ApplicationJob
  # The message may be deleted before the job runs, in which case there's nothing to tell the bots.
  discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError

  def perform(message)
    message.mentioned_bots_with_webhooks.each do |bot|
      Bot::Webhook.new(bot, message).deliver
    end
  end
end
EOF

class Message < ApplicationRecord
  include Attachment, Broadcasts, Mentionee, Pagination, Searchable

  belongs_to :room, touch: true
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  has_many :boosts, dependent: :destroy

  has_rich_text :body

  before_create -> { self.client_message_id ||= Random.uuid }
  after_create_commit -> { room.receive(self) }
  after_create_commit :trigger_bot_webhooks_later

  scope :ordered, -> { order(:created_at) }
  scope :with_creator, -> { preload(creator: :avatar_attachment) }
  scope :with_attachment_details, -> {
    with_rich_text_body_and_embeds
    with_attached_attachment
      .includes(attachment_blob: :variant_records)
  }
  scope :with_boosts, -> { includes(boosts: :booster) }

  def plain_text_body
    body.to_plain_text.presence || attachment&.filename&.to_s || ""
  end

  def to_key
    [ client_message_id ]
  end

  def content_type
    case
    when attachment?    then "attachment"
    when sound.present? then "sound"
    else                     "text"
    end.inquiry
  end

  def sound
    plain_text_body.match(/\A\/play (?<name>\w+)\z/) do |match|
      Sound.find_by_name match[:name]
    end
  end

  private
    # The webhooks run in a job, so the person posting the message never waits on a bot.
    def trigger_bot_webhooks_later
      Bot::WebhookJob.perform_later(self) if may_mention_anyone?
    end
end
EOF

steps.message: Next, the docs. `docs/bots.md` is the feature's design note, so the webhook behavior, delivery rules, and operating trade-offs belong there. I'll insert a Webhooks section before "Security notes" and update the form and security bullets, using a Ruby script to avoid shell-quoting problems.

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > /tmp/webhooks_section.md <<'EOF' ## Webhooks A bot can have a **webhook URL** (optional, "Webhook URL" on the bot form; leaving it blank removes the webhook). When a message mentions the bot, Campfire POSTs a JSON description of the mention to that URL. The bot can answer in the HTTP response, or later over the HTTP API. ### When it's called - A message mentions the bot. The @-mention autocomplete inserts the mention, and that's what triggers the webhook. - The bot is active, has a webhook, and is a member of the room the message was posted to. A bot that has left the room isn't called. - Messages written by bots never call webhooks. A bot's reply can mention another bot, and that would set off a loop. - A message that mentions a bot twice calls it once. - Calls run in `Bot::WebhookJob`, after the message is saved, so the person posting never waits for them. A message deleted before its job runs is dropped. Each request is a `POST` with `Content-Type: application/json`: ```json { "event": "mention", "author": { "id": 7, "name": "Alice" }, "room": { "id": 5, "name": "Ops", "reply_to": "/rooms/5//messages" }, "message": { "id": 118, "body": { "text": "restart the build please", "html": "
…
" }, "link": "/rooms/5/@118" } } ``` - `event` is always `mention` for now. More event types may come later, so check it. - `room.name` is the room's name. Direct rooms have no name, so they're named after the people in them other than the bot. - `message.body.text` is the message as plain text, with the bot's own mention removed. Other people's mentions stay as `@Name`. Removing the mention doesn't tidy the whitespace around it, so "hey @Deploy Bot restart" reads "hey restart". - `message.body.html` is the full rich-text body as the app renders it, sanitized. It still includes the bot's mention. - `room.reply_to` is the bot's own posting URL for the room. It's the same path as the HTTP API, so the bot can reply later. **It contains the bot's code**, so whoever receives the payload holds the bot's credential. - `message.link` opens the room scrolled to the message. - Paths are relative. The bot knows its own Campfire origin. ### Answering | Response | What happens | |---------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `200`, `Content-Type: text/plain` | The body is posted into the room as the bot's message. It's escaped and line breaks are kept, as HTTP API text is. | | `200`, `Content-Type: text/html` | The body is posted as the bot's rich text. It's cleaned with the filters messages are shown with, and attachments (mentions included) are dropped, so a bot can't ping people. | | `204` | Nothing is posted. | | Any other status or content type, or empty | Nothing is posted. The outcome is logged, without the URL or the code. | A reply goes into the room the mention came from, and only while the bot is still a member of it. ### Delivery rules - Timeouts: 5 seconds to connect, 10 seconds to write and to read. A bot that needs longer should answer `204` and post later with `reply_to`. - The address is checked with `RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard`, the same as link unfurling. `SECURITY.md` makes this a requirement: a member must not reach the server's private network through Campfire. Loopback, private, link-local and unresolvable addresses are refused. The check happens when a webhook is called, not when the form is saved, since DNS can change. So a bot running on `localhost` can't receive webhooks, even in development. - The connection goes to the address that was checked, so DNS can't change it in between. - Redirects aren't followed. - A reply is capped at 1 MB. The body is read in chunks, and an oversized reply is abandoned rather than buffered. - Only a `200` reply's body is read. Other responses' bodies aren't. - A reply's `charset` is honored. UTF-8 is assumed otherwise. - There are no retries. A failed call is logged and dropped. ### Operating notes - Webhook jobs run on the default queue, which push notifications use too. A slow bot holds a worker for up to about 10 seconds per call. If that becomes a problem, give webhook jobs their own queue and workers in `config/resque-pool.yml`. - Payloads aren't signed, so a receiver can't yet check that a request came from Campfire. Signing (an HMAC over the body with a per-bot secret, say) is the natural next step. - The webhook URL is stored as-is, like the code. It's shown only to the bot's creator and to administrators, on the edit page, which is marked `turbo-cache-control: no-cache`. It can carry secrets in its query string, so treat it like the code. EOF cat > /tmp/update_docs.rb <<'EOF' path = "/app/docs/bots.md" doc = File.read(path) section = File.read("/tmp/webhooks_section.md") marker = "## Security notes\n" raise "marker missing" unless doc.include?(marker) doc = doc.sub(marker, section + marker) old_form = "- `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit` share one form: avatar (optional), name (\"Name the bot\", required), \"Save changes\".\n The edit page adds \"Delete this chat bot\", which asks for confirmation with Turbo's `data-turbo-confirm`\n (the native `confirm()`)." raise "form bullet missing" unless doc.include?(old_form) new_form = "- `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit` share one form: avatar (optional), name (\"Name the bot\", required), webhook URL\n (optional, \"Webhook URL\", see [Webhooks](#webhooks)), \"Save changes\".\n The edit page adds \"Delete this chat bot\", which asks for confirmation with Turbo's `data-turbo-confirm`\n (the native `confirm()`)." doc = doc.sub(old_form, new_form) old_sec = "- Bot text is HTML-escaped before it's stored, so bots can't inject markup into other people's pages.\n" raise "security bullet missing" unless doc.include?(old_sec) new_sec = old_sec + "- Webhook payloads carry the code in `room.reply_to`, which is how a bot replies, so a webhook's receiver holds the\n credential. Campfire's own log lines name the bot by id only, never its code or webhook URL.\n- Webhook URLs must be `http` or `https`, and are subject to the same private-address check as link unfurling (see\n [Webhooks](#webhooks)).\n" doc = doc.sub(old_sec, new_sec) File.write(path, doc) puts "ok" EOF ruby /tmp/update_docs.rb && grep -n "^## \|^### " docs/bots.md

steps.message:
Most of the browser checks pass:

- The Webhook URL field has the right type, placeholder, and label, and it wraps the input.
- An `ftp://` URL is refused with the expected message.

The confirmation behaves correctly. Clicking Delete raises a native dialog with the expected message. Dismissing keeps the bot on the edit page. Accepting deletes it and returns to `/bots`.

While reviewing the reply decoding for this check, I spotted a real bug. `encode(UTF_8, ...)` is a no-op when the source is already UTF-8, so invalid bytes would survive into `html_escape`, which raises on them. A bot could then crash the job with a non-network exception. I'll confirm that with a test before fixing it.

require "restricted_http/private_network_guard"

# Calls a bot's webhook when a message mentions the bot, and posts what the bot answers with:
#
# - 200 with text/plain or text/html: the body is posted into the room as the bot's message.
# - 204, or any other status: nothing is posted. A bot that wants to reply later can post over the bot API, using the
#   reply_to path in the payload.
#
# Bot::WebhookJob runs this, so a slow or broken webhook never holds up the person who posted the message.
class Bot::Webhook
  OPEN_TIMEOUT = 5 # seconds
  READ_TIMEOUT = 10 # seconds
  MAX_REPLY_SIZE = 1.megabyte
  REPLY_CONTENT_TYPES = %w[ text/plain text/html ]

  # Raised while reading a reply that's too big, to abandon the rest of the response.
  class ReplyTooLarge < StandardError; end

  # Failures reaching a bot are expected, so they're logged rather than retried. Anything else is a bug and raises.
  UNREACHABLE_ERRORS = [
    Timeout::Error, SocketError, SystemCallError, IOError, OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError,
    Net::ProtocolError, Net::HTTPBadResponse, Zlib::Error,
    RestrictedHTTP::Violation, Surfguard::Unresolvable
  ]

  attr_reader :bot, :message

  def initialize(bot, message)
    @bot, @message = bot, message
  end

  def deliver
    reply = fetch_reply

    post_reply(reply) if reply.present? && bot_in_room?
  rescue ReplyTooLarge, *UNREACHABLE_ERRORS => e
    Rails.logger.warn "Webhook for bot #{bot.id} produced no reply: #{e.class} #{e.message}"
  end

  private
    def url
      @url ||= URI.parse(bot.webhook_url)
    end

    # The address is checked and then pinned, so the connection goes to the address that was checked, even if DNS
    # changes in between. Redirects aren't followed, so a bot can't send us somewhere that wasn't checked.
    def fetch_reply
      ip = RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard.resolve(url.host)

      Net::HTTP.start(url.host, url.port, ipaddr: ip, use_ssl: url.scheme == "https",
          open_timeout: OPEN_TIMEOUT, read_timeout: READ_TIMEOUT, write_timeout: READ_TIMEOUT) do |http|
        http.request(build_request) do |response|
          # Returning from inside the block means the body of anything but a 200 is never read.
          return response.is_a?(Net::HTTPOK) ? reply_html(response) : nil
        end
      end
    end

    def build_request
      Net::HTTP::Post.new(url, "Content-Type" => "application/json").tap do |request|
        request.body = Bot::Webhook::Payload.new(bot, message).to_json
      end
    end

    def reply_html(response)
      return unless REPLY_CONTENT_TYPES.include?(response.content_type&.downcase)

      text = decode(read_reply(response), response.type_params["charset"])

      if response.content_type.downcase == "text/html"
        Bot.html_from_html(text)
      else
        Bot.html_from_text(text)
      end
    end

    def read_reply(response)
      body = +""

      response.read_body do |chunk|
        body << chunk
        raise ReplyTooLarge if body.bytesize > MAX_REPLY_SIZE
      end

      body
    end

    # Falls back to UTF-8 when the reply names no charset, or one Ruby doesn't know.
    def decode(body, charset)
      encoding = Encoding.find(charset || "UTF-8") rescue Encoding::UTF_8

      body.force_encoding(encoding).encode(Encoding::UTF_8, invalid: :replace, undef: :replace)
    end

    # A bot that was removed from the room since the mention can't post into it, the same as over the bot API.
    def bot_in_room?
      bot.user.rooms.exists?(message.room_id)
    end

    def post_reply(html)
      # Only bot messages with visible text are posted. A reply of nothing but markup is left out.
      return unless ActionText::Content.new(html).to_plain_text.present?

      message.room.messages.create!(creator: bot.user, body: html).tap(&:broadcast_create)
    end
end
"
}

- **The code is a credential.** It's 24 random base58 characters (`has_secure_token`), unique, and stored as-is,
  because the list has to show it. Anyone who holds it can post as the bot, so:
  - It's only shown to the bot's creator and to administrators, on `/bots`. Edit and delete pages don't show it.
  - It travels in the URL path, which is why it's masked everywhere a path or URL gets recorded:
    - Request logs: `lib/rails_ext/request_filtered_path.rb` prepends to `ActionDispatch::Request#filtered_path`,
      and `BotCodeFilter` masks `/rooms/:id/<code>/messages`. Parameter logs mask `code` (`filter_parameter_logging.rb`).
    - Sentry: `config/initializers/sentry.rb` scrubs the request URL in `before_send`.
  - Deactivating a user, or banning one, stops its bots from authenticating (`Bot.authenticate` only accepts active users).
- The endpoint is outside the session and CSRF machinery: `allow_unauthenticated_access`, `skip_forgery_protection`.
- Rails' parameter parsing is skipped for the body (`Bots::MessagesController#process_action`). Otherwise Rails parses
  form bodies (`100% done` is an invalid form, so it gets a 400) and JSON bodies (malformed JSON gets a 400). Multipart
  requests are still parsed, for the attachment.
- Bot text is HTML-escaped before it's stored, so bots can't inject markup into other people's pages.
- Webhook payloads carry the code in `room.reply_to`, which is how a bot replies, so a webhook's receiver holds the
  credential. Campfire's own log lines name the bot by id only, never its code or webhook URL.
- Webhook URLs must be `http` or `https`, and are subject to the same private-address check as link unfurling (see
  [Webhooks](#webhooks)).

- The code isn't encrypted at rest. The app doesn't configure Active Record encryption keys, and the code has to be

  deterministic encryption.
- There's no way to rotate a code yet. Deleting and recreating the bot is the workaround. A "Regenerate code" action

steps.message:
The webhook feature is in place, the full suite passes, and the scratch files are gone. Everything is uncommitted in the working tree.

## What I built

- **Webhook URL on bots.** New migration adds `bots.webhook_url`. The bot form (`/bots/new` and edit) has a "Webhook URL" field, which is a `type=url` input with a wrapping `<label>`. Blank saves as no webhook. Anything that isn't an http(s) URL with a host is rejected.
- **Mention → callback.** After a message is created, a job is enqueued only if the body contains a mention attachment. That check is in-memory, so the poster's request does no HTTP and no extra lookups. `Bot::WebhookJob` then calls each mentioned bot that has a webhook, is active, and is a member of the room.
- **Payload.** Matches the story's format: `event`, `author`, `room` (`id`, `name`, `reply_to`), and `message` (`id`, `body.text` with the bot's own mention removed, `body.html`, `link`). Paths are relative.
- **Replies.** A 200 with `text/plain` is escaped and posted as the bot. A 200 with `text/html` is cleaned with the same filters messages use, and attachments are dropped so a bot can't ping people. A 204 posts nothing. Any other outcome posts nothing and is logged without the URL or code.
- **Delivery safeguards.** Connect timeout 5s, read/write 10s. The address is checked with `RestrictedHTTP::PrivateNetworkGuard` and the connection is pinned to that address. Redirects are not followed. Replies are capped at 1 MB.
- **Autocomplete.** Bots already appeared in the mention autocomplete because they are active users. I added regression tests and changed nothing.
- **Docs.** `docs/bots.md` has a new Webhooks section covering the rules, the payload, the reply table, delivery limits, and operating notes.

## Decisions to review

1. **Private and loopback webhook addresses are refused.** `SECURITY.md` puts anything a non-admin can reach through Campfire in scope, and link unfurling already blocks private addresses. A bot pointed at `localhost` will not receive callbacks, even in development. If QA points webhooks at a local receiver, they will fail. Fixing that needs an explicit operator-level allowance, which I did not add.
2. **`reply_to` uses the existing route**, `/rooms/:room_id/:bot_code/messages`. The story's example shows `42-<code>`, but the existing bot API authenticates by code alone, so an id prefix would not resolve.
3. **Bot-authored messages never trigger webhooks.** This prevents two bots from setting each other off. It is an interpretation of "a user mentions a bot".
4. **Only new messages trigger webhooks.** Editing a message to add a mention does not. This matches push notifications.
5. **Shared worker capacity.** Webhook jobs run on the default queue, which push notifications also use. A slow bot can hold a worker for up to about 10 seconds per call. There are no retries and no payload signing. The docs list these as follow-ups.

## Verification

- Full `bin/rails test`: 418 runs, 0 failures, 0 errors. The 22 skips are the same DNS-dependent tests that were skipped at baseline.
- Rubocop reports no offenses across 268 files. Brakeman reports 0 warnings.
- A throwaway test over a real TCP socket (deleted afterwards) confirmed the JSON request, a 200 text/plain reply being posted, a 204, the 10-second read timeout, a 302 not being followed, and an oversized reply being cut off.
- Headless Chromium, driven through Ferrum because chromedriver isn't installed, confirmed: the form labels and validation, clearing the URL, the composer autocomplete listing the bot, a mention posting quickly, the server refusing `localhost` as expected, and the native `confirm()` on delete (dismiss keeps the bot, accept deletes it). System tests themselves did not run.
- Mutation checks: removing the membership check, treating 2xx as success, letting bot-authored messages trigger, and not stripping the bot's own mention each made a test fail.

## Repo notes

- The bots feature was already uncommitted work in this tree. I built on top of it and added a new migration rather than editing `create_bots`.
- I added the attribute name to `config/locales/en.yml` so the error reads "Webhook URL must be an http or https address".
